title: Ki Tavo: coming in, going out (Deuteronomy 28:3–6)
hook: blessed in the city and the field, coming in and going out
tomorrow: Ki Tavo: a heart to know (Deuteronomy 29:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Ki Tavo, hayom: the old commandments, new each day. Your line was this day, new. Today, blessings for every step of an ordinary day.

Count how many thresholds you'll cross today. Out the front door. Into a car or onto a bus. Into work, or school, or a store. Back out. Back home. Most of those crossings take less than a second and leave no memory at all. On the doorframe of a Jewish home there's a small case, a mezuzah, and some people touch it as they pass, going in and going out. The doorway is treated as a place worth a moment. Today's verses bless exactly those crossings, and everything around them.
screen: `COUNT THE DOORWAYS.` → `A HAND ON THE MEZUZAH.` → `THE CROSSINGS, BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy twenty-eight opens with a list of blessings, if the people keep the covenant. It starts small and wide at once: "Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field." Then the children and the herds, the basket and the kneading-trough. And it ends: "Blessed shalt thou be when thou comest in, and blessed shalt thou be when thou goest out." City and field cover where you are. Coming in and going out cover how you move between them. Hardly a moment of the day is left out. The basket and the kneading-trough are kitchen things, where the bread begins; the blessing reaches right into the bowl. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, gives the last verse a second reading. Coming in and going out can mean coming into the world and leaving it: may your leaving be like your arriving, free of wrongdoing. A whole life read as one doorway. A psalm uses the same pair: "The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever." These blessings sit in a hard chapter. They're short, and the curses that follow are long and frightening; by custom the reader chants those quickly and in a lowered voice. But the chapter begins with blessing, and the blessing is about the plainest movements a person makes.
screen: `IN THE CITY, IN THE FIELD.` · `THE BASKET AND THE KNEADING-TROUGH.` · `ARRIVING IN, AND LEAVING, THE WORLD.` · `SHORT BLESSINGS, A HARD CHAPTER.` · then, large: `BLESSED COMING AND GOING.`

segments.voice: Picture the door you'll walk out of next, your hand on it, and a half-second pause before you go through. If you pray, the psalm's words are there: the LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in; if you don't, a breath and a wish that the day goes well will do. Then picture coming back through the same door tonight, and pausing there too.
Ki Tavo. When you come in. The portion where blessing covers the city and the field, the coming in and the going out.
Your line: blessed coming and going. Even the kneading bowl gets a blessing. That's day five hundred fifteen.

chat.says: Why would the Torah bother blessing something as ordinary as walking in and out a door?
options: The blessings cover city and field, coming in and going out, so hardly a moment of the day is left out.
Only the priests' comings and goings at the Temple were blessed; ordinary people weren't included.
The blessing is for the house itself, so it only counts once a new door has been built.
chat.meaning: Deuteronomy 28 blesses you in the city and the field, coming in and going out: the plainest movements of a day, and in the Talmud, a whole life.
